questions.questionText: A dataset is 99.5% "not fraud" and 0.5% "fraud". A model that always predicts "not fraud" scores 99.5% accuracy. What does this demonstrate?
options: The model is excellent and should be deployed
Accuracy can be highly misleading on imbalanced datasets, since a trivial/useless model can still score very high
99.5% accuracy is impossible to achieve any other way
Fraud detection doesn't need any evaluation metric
questions.correctAnswer: Accuracy can be highly misleading on imbalanced datasets, since a trivial/useless model can still score very high
questions.explanation: On imbalanced data, a model that never predicts the rare class can still post a very high accuracy while being completely useless — precision/recall expose this immediately.

options: Of everything predicted positive, what fraction actually was positive
Of everything that was actually positive, what fraction the model correctly caught
The overall accuracy of the model
How fast the model makes predictions
questions.correctAnswer: Of everything that was actually positive, what fraction the model correctly caught
questions.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) — it's about not missing real positive cases, regardless of how many false alarms that costs.

questions.questionText: Why does F1 use the harmonic mean of precision and recall instead of a simple average?
options: The harmonic mean is easier to compute
The harmonic mean sharply penalizes cases where one of precision or recall is very low, even if the other is very high
There's no meaningful difference between the two
F1 doesn't actually use precision or recall
questions.correctAnswer: The harmonic mean sharply penalizes cases where one of precision or recall is very low, even if the other is very high
questions.explanation: A simple average of 100% precision and 1% recall would look like 50.5%, hiding how bad the recall is. The harmonic mean drags the F1 score down toward the smaller value instead.
